title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Deployment Guidelines + Customer Requirements Library
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference guidance for private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It covers: reference architectures, packaging recommendations, pre-install customer requirements, day-2 operational practices, and formal upgrade & rollback procedures. Intended audience: solutions engineers, deployment engineers, SREs, and customer infrastructure teams.

High-level goals
- Provide repeatable, secure VPC and on-prem deployment patterns.
- Capture minimal customer prerequisites and common constraints.
- Standardize day-2 ops and upgrade/rollback playbooks to meet SLA and security commitments.

Scope and assumptions
- Focuses on Redwood Private (VPC/private control plane + optional on-prem runtime).
- Assumes customer provides networking, compute, and KMS/HSM integration where required.
- Where options exist (e.g., cloud vs bare-metal), we document recommended default and fallbacks.

1) Reference architectures (summary)

A. VPC (managed customer cloud account) - recommended for most customers
- Control plane: Redwood-managed control plane endpoints hosted in Redwood; customer access via peered VPC endpoints or private link.
- Data plane (model serving): Customer-owned VPC with Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS) or managed VM pool connected to GPU instances.
- Key components: NAT/egress, private subnets for serving nodes, internal load balancer, metrics/observability collectors in isolated subnets, optional transit gateway for multi-region.
- Network patterns: restrict egress to Redwood control plane IPs + required external services; use Security Groups / NSGs to restrict ports (gRPC/HTTP ports only).

B. On-prem (air-gapped or limited egress) - used for regulated workloads
- Control plane: optional private control plane hosted in customer network; for air-gapped, deploy full control + data plane on customer infrastructure.
- Packaging: container images + offline tarball of model artifacts and runtime binaries; automated installer (Ansible/ssh) and local package repository.
- Storage: NFS/SMB or local NVMe depending on performance needs; model cache on local NVMe recommended for low-latency workloads.

2) Minimal customer requirements (pre-sales checklist)
- Networking
  - CIDR blocks for the VPC and any subnets (private and management).
  - Firewall/IP allowlist for Redwood control plane (if used) and management CIDR for operator access.
  - NAT/egress for cluster nodes or approved egress proxy for controlled updates.
- Compute & capacity
  - GPU type and counts (e.g., a100-80gb, h100-80gb, or sku equivalent). Provide expected peak RPS and token/sec workload to size clusters.
  - Minimum node specs for control plane components (cpu/memory/disk).
- Identity & secrets
  - KMS/HSM integration details and principals or service account used for envelope encryption.
  - SAML/SCIM identity provider for operator logins (optional but recommended).
- Storage and model artifacts
  - Model artifact storage location (S3-compatible endpoint or on-prem object store) and access keys.
  - Persistent volume requirements (size, IOPS) for runtime cache and logs.
- Compliance and security
  - Required audit logging retention and any restricted ports/protocols.
  - Data residency constraints and encryption-at-rest KPIs.

Customer readiness matrix (quick yes/no)
- [ ] Network CIDRs + peering config available
- [ ] GPU quota requested and approved
- [ ] KMS/HSM access provided
- [ ] Artifact store credentials validated
- [ ] Operator access method defined (VPN/Bastion/SAML)

3) Packaging recommendations (on-prem)
- Provide an offline bundle: runtime.tar.gz containing "images/" (OCI tarballs), "artifacts/" (models), "tools/installer.sh" and a signed manifest (SHA256).
- Installer model: idempotent Ansible playbooks + systemd units for Redwood services. Example install command:

  ./installer.sh --bundle /tmp/runtime.tar.gz --inventory /etc/redwood/inventory.yml --mode offline

- Container runtime: support both containerd and Docker Engine; prefer containerd for production.
- Image signing: all images must be signed; installer validates signatures against provided public key.

4) Day-2 operations (runbook highlights)

Common day-2 tasks
- Health checks and SLO monitoring
  - Primary SLOs: per-model p99 latency <= customer SLO, availability >= 99.9% (example).
  - Alerts: node GPU utilization > 85% for 10m, model OOMs > 3 in 5m, request queue length > threshold.
- Capacity scaling
  - Autoscaler tune: target CPU < 70% and GPU memory headroom > 10% per node class.
  - Manual scale: add GPU node pool (preferred) and let autoscaler rebalance.
- Model cache management
  - Cache eviction: LRU with reserved space for pinned models. Use maintenance window for cache warmups.
- Log rotation & retention
  - Use centralized logging (Fluentd/Vector) to push to customer ELK/Splunk; keep node local logs for 7 days and store aggregated logs for retention required by compliance.

Day-2 runbook: common incident scenarios
1. High latency across requests
  1) Confirm whether latency is compute (GPU saturation) vs tail (KV cache misses) vs network.
  2) Check dashboards: p50/p95/p99, GPU util, network egress.
  3) Actions: increase node pool, pin hot models to local cache, enable warmup policy.
2. Model deployment failed (OOM or invalid weights)
  1) Roll back to previous model revision via canary abort (see upgrade playbook).
  2) If persistent OOMs, change model variant (smaller quantization/sequence length limits).
3. Node failure (hardware or driver)
  1) Reboot node via orchestration. If not recoverable, cordon + drain and replace node from image build.

5) Upgrade & rollback procedure (formal, numbered)

Purpose: safe model/runtime/software upgrades with automated rollback and minimal customer impact. Applies to control plane patches, runtime container updates, and model rollouts.

Preconditions
- Backups of control plane DB and model artifact store snapshot completed.
- Canary environment configured and smoke tests passing.
- Change approved in change management with rollback plan documented.

Upgrade steps (runtime or control plane)
1. Prepare release bundle and release notes; sign the bundle.
2. Deploy to staging/canary (10% of traffic or dedicated canary nodes). Run full smoke and perf tests (latency, throughput, key endpoint checks).
3. If tests pass, rollout to 25% of capacity and monitor for 30 minutes. Key signals: error rate, p99 latency, GPU OOMs, request queue length.
4. If healthy, continue to 100% in incremental steps (25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 100%) with at least 15-30 minute observation windows.
5. Post-upgrade validation: run synthetic workload (provided test suite) for 1 hour and verify telemetry baselines.

Rollback steps (if any gateway signal fails)
1. Immediately stop the rollout and shift incoming traffic back to the last healthy revision (automated via routing policy).
2. If automated rollback fails, execute manual restore from snapshot for control plane services.
3. Open an incident, attach logs, and notify customers per SLA.

Model rollout specifics (canaries and safety nets)
- Canary ratio: default 5-10% for critical models, 10-25% for non-critical.
- Automatic abort thresholds: error rate increase > 1% absolute AND > 2x baseline OR p99 latency regression > 30%.
- Safety nets: automatic fallback to previous revision, and global rate limit throttle applied while investigating.

6) Packaging of runbooks and operational artifacts
- Store runbooks as YAML metadata + markdown steps in the runbook repo (git) and sync to Confluence pages.
- Example runbook entry header (YAML front matter style):

---
name: node-replacement
severity: high
owner: eng-sre
---

7) Customer requirements library (sample entries)

- Requirement: GPU quota and instance type
  - Detail: Customer must provision GPU instances (A100/H100 or equivalent). Provide a minimum of N nodes for baseline throughput.
  - Validation: Solutions engineer runs perf harness and validates p95/p99.

- Requirement: Private artifact store (S3 compatible)
  - Detail: Provide endpoint, access key, and read-only role for model pulls. Signed URLs acceptable for offline installs.
  - Validation: Installer successfully pulls model artifacts in a staging environment.

- Requirement: KMS integration
  - Detail: Provide KMS key ARN or HSM provisioning steps to enable envelope encryption for model artifacts and logs.
  - Validation: Exchange a test ciphertext and perform successful decrypt during install.

8) Templates & CLI snippets

Network peering (AWS example)
- Example peering and route command snippets (customer):
  aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id vpc-01234 --peer-vpc-id vpc-56789 --peer-region us-west-2

Installer check (on-prem)
- Verify image signatures:
  ./installer.sh --verify-signature /tmp/runtime.tar.gz --pubkey /etc/redwood/pubkey.pem

Canary abort policy (example config snippet)
- JSON example used by routing controller: 
  {
    "abort_conditions": ["error_rate>1%", "p99_latency>30%"]
  }

9) Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments team.
- Oncall escalation: eng-sre -> eng-platform -> eng-serving-runtime.
- Contact: private-deployments-support@redwood.com (internal)

10) Related artifacts and pages
- Link to deployment runbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-vpc-onprem-deployment-runbook-2028-03-01
- Link to packaging guidelines: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-vpc-onprem-reference-packaging-day2-ops-2026-03-04

Appendix: Performance sizing quick reference
- Small: 4 x A100-40GB, expected baseline 100 rps (varies by model).
- Medium: 8 x A100-80GB, expected baseline 300 rps.
- Large: 16+ x H100, used for high throughput or multi-tenant clusters.
